Berries
bĕr´ĭz
n. pl. (the fruit of the olive; what is left after the shaking — Hebrew gargar)
Old English berie, a small fruit. In both scriptural uses the berries are olives — the Hebrew gargar is the olive berry left on the bough after the tree is beaten.

Biblical Definition

Berries in the Authorized Version are olives, and both occurrences are doctrinal. Isaiah describes what will be left of a nation under judgment: “Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outmost fruitful branches thereof, saith the LORD God of Israel” (Isa 17:6). The picture is exact and it is a picture of the remnant. When an olive tree is beaten at harvest, a few berries always remain out of reach at the very top and on the far ends of the branches, and the poor came after and gleaned them by the law of God. So it will be with Israel: not a total end, but two or three in the top of the uppermost bough, left by God's own appointment. James uses the olive berry for a different point: “Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs? so can no fountain both yield salt water and fresh” (Jas 3:12), following his question, “Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?” (Jas 3:11). A tree bears after its kind, and a tongue speaks out of what a man is. Blessing God and cursing men out of the same mouth is a botanical impossibility dressed as religion.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a berry as a succulent or pulpy fruit containing naked seeds; and notes the scriptural use of the olive berry, the fruit of the olive tree.

expand to see more

BER'RY, n. A succulent or pulpy fruit containing naked seeds.

2. In the Scriptures, the fruit of the olive tree; as, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough.

OL'IVE, n. A plant or tree of the genus Olea, of great value for its fruit and the oil expressed from it.

GLEAN, v.t. To gather the stalks and ears of grain, or the fruit left after the harvest.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 17:6 — "Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outmost fruitful branches thereof, saith the LORD God of Israel."

James 3:12 — "Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs? so can no fountain both yield salt water and fresh."

James 3:11 — "Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?"

Romans 11:17 — "And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;"

Modern Corruption

Speech is treated as separable from character, so that a man may be judged by his convictions while his tongue is excused as temperament.

expand to see more

James 3 is built on the impossibility of a divided nature producing divided fruit, and the olive berry is his final illustration. A fig tree cannot bear olives; a fountain cannot give sweet and bitter at the same place. From which he concludes that a mouth which blesses God and curses men made in God's likeness is testifying against itself. The modern separation of a man's doctrine from his speech — sound convictions excusing a savage tongue, or a pleasant manner excusing false teaching — is precisely what James forbids. Both come out of the same root, and the root is what is actually being reported.

Isaiah's berries carry the doctrine of the remnant, and it must not be softened in either direction. The judgment is real: the tree is beaten, and what is left is two or three berries at the top. But the leaving is God's doing and it is stated by name — saith the LORD God of Israel. Paul takes up the same olive tree in Romans 11 to say that branches were broken off and a wild olive graffed in, and to warn the graffed branch not to boast against them. Where Gentile Christians read the remnant as Israel's failure rather than God's preservation, they take exactly the posture Paul forbids: thou bearest not the root, but the root thee.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gargar (H1620), an olive berry — Isaiah 17:6 only; Greek elaia (G1636), an olive or olive tree; pege (G4077), a fountain, in James 3:11.

expand to see more

Hebrew gargar (H1620) — a berry of the olive; Isaiah 17:6, its only occurrence.

Greek elaia (G1636) — olive tree or fruit; James 3:12, Romans 11:17, and the mount of Olives.

Greek pege (G4077) — a fountain, spring; James 3:11, and John 4:14 of the well of water springing up.

Deuteronomy 24:20 commanded that when the olive was beaten, the boughs were not to be gone over again — the remainder was for the stranger, the fatherless and the widow.

Isaiah's two or three berries in the uppermost bough are the prophets' standing figure of the remnant.

Usage

"“Two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough” — the remnant, left by name."

"“Can the fig tree bear olive berries?” — and neither can a divided mouth."

"The berries out of reach were the gleaner's portion by the law."
